'''thew<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''thew'', ''theow'', < AS. ''theów'' = OHG. ''diu'' = Goth. ''thius'', a bondman, slave, servant. Cf. ''thane''.] A bondman; a slave.

{{smaller block|Miȝti men & menskful were thei in here time,
& feithful as here fader to fre & to ''thewe''.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 5514.}}}}

'''thew<sup>1</sup>†''', ''a.'' [ME., < AS. ''theów'', servile, < ''theów'', a bondman, servant: see ''thew''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] Bond; servile.

'''thew<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v.'' [ME. ''thewen'', < AS. ''thēwan'', ''thȳwan'', ''theówan'' (= MD. ''douwen'' = MLG. ''duwen'' = MHG. ''diuhen'', ''dūhen'', ''diuwen''), oppress, < ''theów'', a bondman: see ''thew''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] To oppress; enslave.

'''thew<sup>2</sup>†''' (thū), ''n.'' [< ME. ''thew'', earlier ''theaw'', usually in pl. ''thewes'', < AS. ''theáw'', custom, manner, behavior, = OS. ''thau'' = OHG. ''dau'', *''thau'', also *''gadau'', ''kathau'', discipline. Cf. ''thew''<sup>3</sup>.] Custom; habit; manner; usually in the plural, customs; habits; manners; morals; qualities; moral traits; conditions.

{{smaller block|Leue sone, this lessoun me lerde my fader,
that knew of kourt the ''thewes'', for kourteour was he long.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 342.}}}}

{{smaller block|Nathelees it oghte ynough suffise
With any wyf, if so were that she hadde
Mo goode ''thewes'' than hire vices badde.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant's Tale, l. 298.}}}}

'''thew<sup>3</sup>''' (thū), ''n.'' [Usually in the plural ''thews''; a transferred use of ''thews'', manner, bearing, hence bodily form, appearance as showing strength; pl. of ''thew''<sup>2</sup>; or simply a development of the rare ME. sense 'strength' of the same ''thew''<sup>2</sup>.] A muscle; a sinew: used generally in the plural.

{{smaller block|Of maine and of ''theauwe''.}}

{{smaller block|Ffro ''thethen'' the lycour belyue launchit doun evyn.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 8790.}}}}

'''thetic''' (thet′ik), ''a.'' [< Gr. θετικός, positive; cf. θέσις, a laying down, < ''τιθέναι'' (√ ''θε''), put, place: see ''thesis''.] In ''anc. pros.'': (''a'') Pertaining to the thesis, or metrically accented part of a foot. (''b'') Beginning with a thesis: opposed to ''anacrustic''.

[[File:century v08 p0090 c1f1.png|center|179px]]
{{c|the Pacific islands, and ''Thespesia populnea''.}}

¶
'''thetical†''' (thet′i-kal), ''a.'' [< ''thetic'' + ''-al''.] Laid down; prescriptive; arbitrary.

{{smaller block|This law that prohibited Adam the eating of the fruit was merely ''thetical'' or positive, not indispensable and natural.
{{right|''Dr. H. More'', Def. of Lit. Cabbala, ii.}}}}

'''Thetis''' (thē′tis), ''n.'' [< L. ''Thetis'', < Gr. Θέτις: see def.] 1. In ''classical myth.'', a marine goddess, who became the spouse of the mortal Peleus, despite her efforts to escape him by countless Protean transformations, and was by him the mother of Achilles.—2. The seventeenth planetoid, discovered by Luther at Bilk in 1852.

'''thetsee''' (thet′sē), ''n.'' Same as ''theetsee''.

'''theurgic''' (thē-ėr′jik), ''a.'' [= F. ''théurgique'' = Sp. ''teúrgico'' = Pg. ''theurgico'' = It. ''teurgico'', < LL. ''theurgicus'', < Gr. θεουργικός, < θεουργία, theurgy: see ''theurgy''.] Pertaining to theurgy, or the power of performing supernatural things.

{{smaller block|The soul of the mystic would have passed into the world of spiritual existences; but he was not yet blessed with ''theurgic'' faculties, and patiently awaited for the elect.
{{right|''I. D'Israeli'', Amen. of Lit., II. 294.}}}}

'''Theurgic hymns''' or '''songs''', songs used in incantation.

'''theurgical''' (thē-ėr′ji-kal), ''a.'' [< ''theurgic'' + ''-al''.] Same as ''theurgic''.

'''theurgist''' (thē′ėr-jist), ''n.'' [= F. ''théurgiste''; as ''theurg-y'' + ''-ist''.] One who believes in theurgy, or practises a pretended magic.

{{smaller block|As if there be any irrational demons, as the ''theurgists'' affirm.
{{right|''Cudworth'', Intellectual System, p. 864.}}}}

'''theurgy''' (thē′ėr-ji), ''n.'' [= F. ''théurgie'' = Sp. ''teurgia'' = Pg. ''theurgia'' = It. ''teurgia'', < LL. ''theurgia'', < LGr. θεουργία, a divine work, a miracle, magic, sorcery, < θεουργός, one who does the works of God, a priest, < Gr. θεός, god, + *ἔργειν, work.] The working of some divine or supernatural agency in human affairs; a producing of effects by supernatural means; effects or phenomena brought about among men by spiritual agency. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') Divine agency, or direct divine interference, in human affairs or the government of the world.}}

{{smaller block|Homer, with the vast mechanism of the Trojan war in his hands, and in such hands, and almost compelled to employ an elaborate and varied ''theurgy'', . . . was in a position of advantage without parallel for giving form to the religious traditions of his country.
{{right|''Gladstone.''}}}}

{{smaller block|(''b'') A system of supernatural knowledge or powers believed by the Egyptian Platonists and others to have been communicated to mankind by the beneficent deities, and to have been handed down from generation to generation traditionally by the priests. (''c'') The art of invoking deities or spirits, or by their intervention conjuring up visions, interpreting dreams, prophesying, receiving and explaining oracles, etc.; the supposed power of obtaining from the gods, by means of certain observances, words, symbols, etc., a knowledge of the secrets which surpass the powers of reason—a power claimed by the priesthood of most pagan religions.}}

{{smaller block|Porphyry and some others did distinguish these two sorts, so as to condemn indeed the grosser, which they called magick or goety; but allowed the other, which they termed ''theurgy'', as laudable and honourable, and as an art by which they received angels, and had communication with the gods.
{{right|''Hallywell'', Melampronœa (1682), p. 51.}}}}

{{smaller block|It may appear a subject of surprise and scandal . . . that the Grecian mysteries should have been supported by the magic or ''theurgy'' of the modern Platonists.
{{right|''Gibbon'', Decline and Fall, xxiii.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''d'') In ''mod. magic'', the pretended production of effects by supernatural agency, as contradistinguished from natural magic.}}

'''thevet†''', ''n.'' [ME.; cf. ''thevethorn''.] Bramble.

{{smaller block|''Theve'', brusch [var. ''there'', brusch].
{{right|''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 490.}}}}

'''theve-thorn†''', ''n.'' [ME., also ''theovethorn'', also ''thethorn'', < AS. ''thēfethorn'', ''thēfanthorn'', ''thīfethorn'', a bramble, Christ's-thorn, < *''thēfe'' (appar. connected with ''thȳfel'', a bush) + ''thorn'', thorn.] A bramble, probably ''Rubus fruticosus''.

{{smaller block|Befor that ȝoure thornes shulden vnderstonde the ''theue thorne''; as the lyuende, so in wrathe he shal soupe them vp.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Ps. lvii. 10.}}}}

'''Thevetia''' (thē-vē′shi-ä), ''n.'' [NL. (Linnæus, 1737), named after André ''Thevet'' (1502–90), a French monk and traveler.] A genus of plants, of the order ''Apocynaceæ'', tribe ''Plumerieæ'', and subtribe ''Cerbereæ''. {{smaller|It is characterized by a glandular calyx and a funnel-shaped corolla with its lobes sinistrorsely overlapping. There are about 4 species, natives of tropical Asia, Madagascar, and the islands of the Pacific. They are smooth shrubs or small trees, with alternate leaves, and large yellow flowers in terminal cymes. For ''T. neriif

'''thew<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''thew'', ''theow'', < AS. ''theów'' = OHG. ''diu'' = Goth. ''thius'', a bondman, slave, servant. Cf. ''thane''.] A bondman; a slave.

& feithful as here fader to fre & to ''thewe''.

'''thew<sup>1</sup>†''', ''a.'' [ME., < AS. ''theów'', servile, < ''theów'', a bondman, servant: see ''thew''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] Bond; servile.

'''thew<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v.'' [ME. ''thewen'', < AS. ''thēwan'', ''thȳwan'', ''theówan'' (= MD. ''douwen'' = MLG. ''duwen'' = MHG. ''diuhen'', ''dūhen'', ''diuwen''), oppress, < ''theów'', a bondman: see ''thew''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] To oppress; enslave.

'''thew<sup>2</sup>†''' (thū), ''n.'' [< ME. ''thew'', earlier ''theaw'', usually in pl. ''thewes'', < AS. ''theáw'', custom, manner, behavior, = OS. ''thau'' = OHG. ''dau'', *''thau'', also *''gadau'', ''kathau'', discipline. Cf. ''thew''<sup>3</sup>.] Custom; habit; manner; usually in the plural, customs; habits; manners; morals; qualities; moral traits; conditions.

{{smaller block|Leue sone, this lessoun me lerde my fader,
that knew of kourt the ''thewes'', for kourteour was he long.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 342.}}}}

{{smaller block|Nathelees it oghte ynough suffise
With any wyf, if so were that she hadde
Mo goode ''thewes'' than hire vices badde.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant's Tale, l. 298.}}}}

'''thew<sup>3</sup>''' (thū), ''n.'' [Usually in the plural ''thews''; a transferred use of ''thews'', manner, bearing, hence bodily form, appearance as showing strength; pl. of ''thew''<sup>2</sup>; or simply a development of the rare ME. sense 'strength' of the same ''thew''<sup>2</sup>.] A muscle; a sinew: used generally in the plural.

{{smaller block|Of maine and of ''theauwe''. {{right|''Layamon'', l. 6361. (''Stratmann.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|Care I for the limb, the ''thewes'', the stature, bulk, and big assemblance of a man! ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iii. 2. 276.}}

{{smaller block|He [must] gain in sweetness and in moral height,
Nor lose the wrestling ''thews'' that throw the world.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, vii.}}}}

'''thew'''<sup>4</sup>† (thū), ''n.'' [ME. ''thewe''; origin obscure.] A cucking-stool; perhaps, also, a form of pillory.

{{smaller block|''Thewe'', or pylory. Collistrigium. ''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 490.}}

{{smaller block|For them [women] the ''thew'' or the tumbrel . . . was reserved. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XIX. 96.}}}}

'''thew'''<sup>5</sup> (thū). An old or provincial or artificial preterit of ''thaw''.

{{smaller block|First it blew,
Then it snew,
Then it ''thew''. {{right|''Old rime.''}}}}

'''thewed'''<sup>1</sup>† (thūd), ''a.'' [< ME. ''thewed''; < ''thew''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Endowed with moral qualities; behaved; mannered.

{{smaller block|Therto so wel fortuned and ''thewed''
That through the world her goodnesse is yshewed.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Complaint of Mars, l. 180.}}}}

{{smaller block|Yet would not seeme so rude, and ''thewed'' ill,
As to despise so curteous seeming part.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. vi. 26.}}}}

'''thewed'''<sup>2</sup> (thūd), ''a.'' [< ''thew''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Having thews, muscle, or strength.

{{smaller block|Till at the last a fearful beast was master,
Amazing ''thewed'', with fourfold plate-like horns.
{{right|''C. De Kay'', Vision of Nimrod, iv.}}}}

'''thewless''' (thū′les), ''a.'' [< ''thew''<sup>3</sup> + ''-less''.] Weak; nerveless.

'''thewy''' (thū′i), ''a.'' [< ''thew''<sup>3</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Sinewy; brawny; muscular.

{{smaller block|There were burly, weather-beaten faces under powder and curls; broad, hard hands in kid gloves; ''thewy'', red elbows, that had plied brooms, shuttles, cards, in lace ruffles.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 10.}}}}

'''they'''<sup>1</sup> (ᴛ̵ʜā), ''pron. pl.'' [< ME. ''they'', ''thei'', ''thai'', partly of Scand. origin (see below), partly < AS. ''thā'' = OS. ''thia'', ''thie'' = OFries. ''thā'' = D. ''de'' = LG. ''de'' = OHG. ''dia'', ''die'', ''de'', MHG. G. ''die'' = Icel. ''their'' = Goth. ''thai''; pl. of AS. ''the'', etc., that, the: see ''that'', ''the''<sup>1</sup>. The ME. ''they'' was declined in midland and southern ME. thus: nom. ''they'', etc., gen. ''hire'', ''here'', ''hir'', ''her'', dat. ''hem''; in northern ME. nom. ''they'', ''thei'', ''thai'', gen. ''thair'', ''thaire'', ''ther'', dat. acc. ''thaim'', ''tham'', ''them''; in Orm. nom. ''theȝȝ'', gen. ''theȝȝre'', dat. acc. ''theȝȝm''; orig. forms of the def. art., AS. nom. acc. pl. ''thā'', gen. ''thāra'', ''thǣra'', dat. ''thǣm'', ''thām''. The AS. ''thā'', ''thāra'', ''thām'' retained the demonstrative force till late in ME.; the northern dialects, however, began through Danish influence to use them, or rather the Danish forms and the AS. forms together, as the plural. Cf. ''he''<sup>1</sup>, ''she'', ''it''. Cf. Icel. nom. ''their'', gen. ''theira'', gen. dat. ''theim'', they, their, them, as the pl. of ''hann'', ''hōn'', he, she.] The plural pronoun of the third person. {{smaller|It stands for a plural noun or pronoun preceding, or in place of one not expressed when pointed out by the situation. It is without gender-forms. (''a'') Nom. ''they''.}}

{{smaller block|And when ''thai'' saw the fyr on brede,
In thaire hertis than had ''thai'' drede;
Vnto the quene al gun ''thai'' cry.
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 93.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
